title: Memorial lit up for first time in a century as part of North West Remembrance tributes

input.lead: The spectacle is just one of the many colourful tributes for Remembrance Day across north-west England
input.summary: The spectacle is just one of the many colourful tributes for Remembrance Day across north-west England
input.evidence_text: Memorial lit up for first time in a century as part of North West Remembrance tributes - BBC News Image source, Dave Mort Photography Image caption, The monument has been restored over a period of more than a decade By Lynette Horsburgh North West Published 39 minutes ago A neglected war memorial has been painstakingly restored by volunteers and lit up for the first time in its 104-year history ahead of Remembrance Day. The Grade II* listed Hoylake and West Kirby monument has been transformed thanks to 14 years of renovations by the Friends of Grange Hill and Wirral Borough Council. The spectacle is just one of a range of colourful tributes and events ahead of Remembrance Sunday across north-west England. They include a striking display of thousands of poppies and crosses on a roundabout in Leigh, Greater Manchester, while Poulton-le-Fylde in Lancashire, has a displayed more than a 1,000 yellow poppies to honour "forgotten heroines" who served their country. The Hoylake and West Kirby restoration project began in 2012 after a visitor tried to bring his father, a military veteran, to the memorial but found access virtually impossible. Years of neglect had left the site overgrown while the site's remembrance garden had almost disappeared. Image caption, Events and displays are happening across the region to mark Remembrance Sunday It inspired residents to set up the Friends of Grange Hill group which led the restoration of the memorial and ensure it was accessible to all. The landmark, which is perched on the highest point in West Kirby, will once again play a central role in community commemorations as it hosts West Kirby's Remembrance parade. But, for the first time, wreaths laid in honour of the fallen will be illuminated in the evening by new bespoke lighting. Image s

title: Carrington relief road approved despite hundreds of objections

input.lead: The new road aims to reduce congestion on the single existing road in and out of Carrington in Trafford
input.summary: The new road aims to reduce congestion on the single existing road in and out of Carrington in Trafford
input.evidence_text: Carrington relief road approved despite hundreds of objections - BBC News Image caption, The council says Carrington Relief Road will take traffic away from the centre of the village By Richard Stead North West Published 6 November 2026 A controversial relief road plan has been approved despite hundreds of objections. The new road around Carrington in Trafford, first proposed more than a decade ago, will provide a new route to the M60 and reduce congestion in the village, the council said, as well as opening up the area for new housing. About 5,000 new homes could be built on land close to Manchester United's training ground. But objectors said the approval of the scheme was "heartbreaking", and it would have a devastating impact on wildlife. Liz Patel, deputy leader of Trafford Council, said: "This road has been decades in the making and it will offer residents in Partington an alternative route towards the M60. "The existing road is at maximum capacity and, by our modelling, the relief road will reduce congestion in the village of Carrington by 67%, as well as opening up the area for new homes while mitigating the biodiversity along the route." Image caption, Liz Patel, the Deputy Leader of Trafford Council, says the new road will help create new jobs The Carrington Relief Road is set to be a 2.7-mile single carriageway that would link the A6144 Manchester Road to an upgraded junction at Banky Lane/Carrington Spur. Half of the road would cross what is currently open farmland, while the other half would be built on the former Shell petrochemicals site, which closed in the 2000s. input.evidence_text: The buildings in Manchester, developed by Urban Splash between 2000 and 2008, were alleged to have serious defects discovered in inspections after the Grenfell Tower disaster The extent of the defects was disputed but they have been fixed at a cost of more than £60m, with about £51.1m paid from the government's Building Safety Fund (BSF) established after the disaster The buildings were not owned by Urban Splash at the time of the remediation work and no BSF money was paid to it. input.summary: The government's new Digital and Technologies Jobs Plan aims to create 200,000 entry-level jobs over the next decade, recognising the barriers facing employers and the importance of regional organisations in connecting people with opportunities. The government has published its D
input.evidence_text: The government's new Digital and Technologies Jobs Plan aims to create 200,000 entry-level jobs over the next decade, recognising the barriers facing employers and the importance of regional organisations in connecting people with opportunities. The government has published its D The plan acknowledges that the challenge is not simply a shortage of people with digital skills. Entry-level recruitment has become more difficult, with employers increasingly favouring experienced candidates and many graduates and other new entrants struggling to secure their fi Manchester Digital contributed to the development of the plan through its involvement in the government's Digital Skills Council, drawing on its work with employers and education providers across Greater Manchester Around 800,000 digital and technology roles are projected to need filling over the next decade. The plan sets out an ambition to create 200,000 entry-level jobs, including apprenticeships, during that period The plan also addresses how AI is changing workforce requirements and the importance of ensuring people entering the industry have both technical knowledge and practical workplace skills Manchester Digital's 2026 Sector Insights Report highlighted a reduction of around 20% in early-career opportunities, despite continued demand for experienced technology professionals

input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
